basics.name: BOSL2 (Belfry OpenSCAD Library v2)
basics.url: https://github.com/BelfrySCAD/BOSL2 (code and README); documentation wiki at https://github.com/BelfrySCAD/BOSL2/wiki (read here through its raw wiki source, because github.com pages are blocked in this environment)
basics.resource_type: CAD library (an OpenSCAD code library with a large auto-generated reference wiki)
basics.license: BSD 2-Clause (the LICENSE file says 'Copyright (c) 2017-2019, Revar Desmera'; openscad.org also lists it as BSD-2-Clause). This is a permissive licence: the code can be reused, changed and shipped (even commercially) as long as the copyright notice is kept. Linking to the wiki pages is always fine
basics.year: Its predecessor BOSL (v1) dates from 2017 (licence years 2017-2019, repo revarbat/BOSL). BOSL2 was started later as an incompatible rewrite, about 2019 [uncertain]. It is still labelled 'BETA CODE' in the README; version.scad reads BOSL_VERSION = [2,0,759]. The wiki refers to a 2025 GitHub issue (#1679) and Hackaday featured it in February 2025, so it was being updated in 2025-2026 [uncertain on the exact latest date]
basics.access_barrier: none to read the wiki in a browser; to generate parts you need a desktop install of OpenSCAD (2021.01 or later) plus the library, and you have to write a little OpenSCAD code
basics.image_license: The wiki images are renders made automatically from the example code on each page (stored under images/<file>/ in the wiki). No separate image licence is stated; they probably fall under the same BSD-2-Clause terms as the code [uncertain]. Anyone can re-render the same pictures by running the example code themselves
basics.authority_level: community or unvetted (a large, well-known open-source community project started by Revar Desmera, now under the BelfrySCAD organisation with several maintainers; listed on the official openscad.org Libraries page, but not a standard or a peer-reviewed source)

coverage.covers: A very large general OpenSCAD toolkit (51 library files, 959 entries in the function/module index), of which a smaller 'parts library' matters for connections: joiners.scad (half joiners and full joiners that screw together, dovetails, snap pins and sockets, rabbit clips, Hirth face splines); hinges.scad (knuckle hinges with a filament, screw or print-in-place cone pin, living hinges, folding hinges with snap locks); partitions.scad (cutting a big model into two interlocking pieces with jigsaw, dovetail, hammerhead, finger, comb, sawtooth or sine-wave seams); gears.scad (spur, helical, herringbone, internal ring, rack, bevel incl. spiral, crown/face, worm, double-enveloping worm, plus a planetary-gear ratio calculator); threading.scad (ISO/UTS, trapezoidal, ACME, square, buttress, NPT and BSPP pipe, garden hose, ball-screw threads); bottlecaps.scad (PCO-1810, PCO-1881, SPI and mason-jar necks and caps and adapters); screws.scad and screw_drive.scad (screws, nuts, nut traps, drive recesses); cubetruss.scad (snap-together truss clips and joiners); sliders.scad (V-groove rail and slider); modular_hose.scad (ball-and-socket modular hose segments); tripod_mounts.scad (Manfrotto RC2 quick-release plate); ball and linear bearings; NEMA stepper mounts; and hooks.scad. The 'Parts' topic lists 64 entries; about 30-40 modules are directly about joints, fasteners or motion parts
coverage.organisation: By code file (a Table of Contents listing each .scad file and its sections), plus an A-Z index of every function and module, a topic index (158 topics such as Joiners, Hinges, Gears, Threading, Bottles, Screws, Modular Hose, Parts), a cheat sheet and a tutorial list. It is organised like a programming reference, not by what a maker wants to do. A beginner who already knows the word 'dovetail' or 'hinge' can find it quickly through the Topics page; someone who only knows 'I want two parts to click together' has no route in
coverage.scope_match: medium. It generates several clever connection TYPES that fit the scope well (rabbit clips with an optional one-way lock, snap pins, print-in-place hinges, living hinges with snap locks, Hirth couplings, interlocking partition seams, dovetails, a full range of gear types, ball-and-socket hose), but it is a code library, not a catalogue: much of it is general geometry tools, and parts like screws, bearings and bottle threads are standard hardware
coverage.taxonomy_used: No mechanism taxonomy. Grouping is by library file (51 files: constants, transforms, attachments, shapes, masks, ..., threading, screws, screw_drive, bottlecaps, ball_bearings, cubetruss, gears, hinges, joiners, linear_bearings, modular_hose, nema_steppers, polyhedra, sliders, tripod_mounts, walls, wiring, hooks), then sections inside each file. Within joiners.scad the sections are Half Joiners, Full Joiners, Dovetails, Tension Clips and Splines; hinges.scad has Hinges and Snap Locks; gears.scad groups gears (spur, ring, rack, crown, bevel, worm), gear assemblies and dimension calculations
coverage.example_types: Rabbit clip (rabbit-eared snap clip, with optional locking flanges); Snap pin and snap-pin socket (split snap pin, fixed or free-turning); Half joiner / joiner (screw-together interlocking tab joint); Dovetail joint (straight, tapered, rounded 'puzzle piece' style); Hirth joint (Hirth face spline coupling); Knuckle hinge with filament or screw pin; Print-in-place knuckle hinge with interlocking cones; Living hinge (flexure hinge) mask; Folding hinge with snap locks (snap_lock / snap_socket); Jigsaw, dovetail, hammerhead, finger, comb, sawtooth and sine-wave interlocking partition seams; Spur, helical and herringbone gears; Internal ring gear; Rack and pinion; Straight, zerol and spiral bevel gears; Crown gear (face gear); Worm and worm gear, double-enveloping worm; Planetary gear set (ratio calculator); Buttress, ACME, trapezoidal and square threads; Ball screw rod; Bottle neck/cap adapters (PCO-1881, mason jar); Garden hose couplers; Modular ball-and-socket hose; Cube truss snap clip; V-groove rail and slider; Manfrotto RC2 quick-release plate
coverage.making_methods: 3D printing first (FDM: clearances, '$slop' printer calibration, teardrop holes, print-in-place hinges, print orientation notes), and parametric CAD in OpenSCAD generally. Nothing on CNC, woodwork or laser cutting as such, although dovetail slopes follow woodworking practice
coverage.item_count: 959 indexed functions, modules and constants across 51 library files; 64 entries under the 'Parts' topic; about 30-40 connection/mechanism modules (joiners.scad 11, hinges.scad 6, gears.scad about 11 geometry modules plus about 17 calculation functions, partitions.scad 4, threading.scad 20)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: no; self-locking: partly (worm drives are included, but self-locking is not discussed; the rabbit clip's lock=true makes a clip that 'may be irreversible'); hand-release only: yes, sort of (the rabbit clip docs say that leaving an access point in the socket wall gives a clip that locks but can be released by pressing its ears); one-way/ratchet: partly (locking rabbit clips go in easily but block removal; no ratchet or pawl module); indexing/detent: partly (Hirth face spline gives fixed angular positions; no detent module); over-centre: no; compliant: yes (living hinges, snap pins, rabbit clips and snap locks all rely on the part flexing); print-in-place: yes (knuckle_hinge in_place=true with interlocking cones); gear trains/gearboxes: yes, strongly (spur, helical, herringbone, ring, rack, bevel, crown, worm, planetary ratio solver, backlash and profile shift); powered connectors: no (only NEMA stepper motor models and mount masks); adhesive types: no
coverage.entry_structure: Each module has: name and one-line synopsis, topics, 'see also' links, usage signatures, a written description (often several paragraphs of practical advice), an arguments table with defaults, and numbered examples each with the OpenSCAD code and a rendered image; some add labelled dimension figures (e.g. the rabbit clip). Degrees of freedom and strength data are not given
coverage.audience_level: hobbyist to professional (makers who can write OpenSCAD code; the gear section is fairly technical)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low to medium. The explanations of individual parts are clear and practical (e.g. how to tighten a snap pin, why hinges need clearance, what backlash is), and every example has a picture. But you must write OpenSCAD code, the pages are long programming references, and there is no plain-English way to discover which joint you need
usefulness.has_images: yes. Every example has a clean rendered image of the generated geometry (joiners.scad has about 46 images, hinges.scad about 29, gears.scad about 111), plus some dimension diagrams. They are computer renders, not photos of printed parts
usefulness.has_animations: no animations seen on the pages checked (joiners, hinges, gears, constants); the examples are still images [uncertain for the rest of the wiki]
usefulness.gaps: No selector or flow chart; organised by code file, not by need; needs coding skills and a desktop install; no photos of real printed results or strength test data; no torque-limiting, ratchet/pawl, detent, over-centre or cam-lock modules; no powered connectors or adhesives; still beta, with API changes; module anchors on the wiki can change when code is reorganised
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: yes, reasonably. Each file has its own wiki page and each section and module has a stable-looking anchor, e.g. https://github.com/BelfrySCAD/BOSL2/wiki/joiners.scad#section-tension-clips (rabbit clips and snap pins), https://github.com/BelfrySCAD/BOSL2/wiki/hinges.scad and https://github.com/BelfrySCAD/BOSL2/wiki/joiners.scad#section-dovetails. Anchors follow the pattern <file>.scad#module-<name>. Good as a 'make it yourself' link from an entry
usefulness.reusable_data: structured and reusable: all code and the wiki are in Git repositories (BelfrySCAD/BOSL2 and its wiki repo, readable as Markdown), and the docs are generated from comments in the source, so a list of modules, topics and synopses could be scraped from the .scad files or the wiki Markdown. The code is BSD-2-Clause, so the list and even the geometry generators can be reused with attribution
usefulness.maintained: Yes, actively maintained: the wiki references 2025 GitHub issues, Hackaday covered it in February 2025, the README invites people to a developer chat, and Fedora packages it (openscad-bosl2). Still marked beta. Exact latest commit date could not be checked because github.com is blocked here [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Each connection explained with its 'knobs' in plain terms: e.g. the snap pin's tightness is set by 'preload' and 'clearance', the rabbit clip by 'snap' depth and 'compression' - the encyclopedia could list the 2-3 settings that matter for each type. (2) A single printer calibration value ('$slop') with a printable calibration test, which the encyclopedia could recommend before printing any fitted joint. (3) Showing variants side by side (locking vs non-locking clip, filament pin vs print-in-place hinge, dovetail vs jigsaw seam). (4) 'See also' links between related joints. (5) Offering a 'make it yourself' link to a parametric generator on each entry. (6) The partition seam patterns (jigsaw, dovetail, hammerhead, finger, comb) as a neat visual list of ways to split a big print into pieces
usefulness.design_rules_given: yes, for several types: snap pin default clearance 0.2 mm and preload 0.2 mm; rabbit clip default compression 0.1 mm and clearance 0.1 mm, socket about 0.4 mm deeper than the clip, with sizes tested in PLA on a Prusa MK3; knuckle hinge default gap 0.2 mm between segments, clearance 0.15 mm ('a layer thickness or two'), default pin hole for 1.75 mm filament, print-in-place cone angle 45 degrees; living hinge leaves 2 layer heights of material; dovetail slopes 1:4, 1:6 or 1:8 (woodworking standard), $slop added on each side of the socket; modular hose clearance 0.05-0.1 mm in PETG; $slop calibration procedure (typical value e.g. 0.15 mm); gear backlash and profile-shift guidance
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: yes, this is its whole purpose: parametric OpenSCAD modules that generate custom geometry for every part (clips, pins, hinges, dovetails, gears, threads and so on)
usefulness.file_formats: SCAD source; OpenSCAD can then export STL, 3MF, OFF, AMF, SVG and DXF (not STEP). The docs are Markdown wiki pages with PNG renders
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: uses correct engineering names (Hirth face spline, crown/face gear, zerol bevel gear, double-enveloping worm, buttress thread, profile shifting, backlash) and explains them briefly, and the gear section cites tec-science references. It also coins its own names ('rabbit clip', 'half joiner', 'cubetruss') that are not standard terms
usefulness.decision_support: none: no selector, flow chart or comparison table. The nearest thing is prose advice inside each module (e.g. rabbit clip vs snap pin: 'unlike the snap pin, this clip is rectangular and can be made at any height') and 'see also' cross-links
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Successor to BOSL v1 (revarbat/BOSL, 2017, not compatible). Overlaps MCAD (gears, nuts and bolts), NopSCADlib (hinges, gears, vitamins) and threads.scad, all listed on openscad.org/libraries.html. Its gear maths follows the tec-science.com references it cites. Cite BOSL2 itself for its clip and joiner designs, which are original to the library
